title: The Sharpe Pint: Warsh's Warning, OpCo Splits, and the Five Sins of Financial AI

opening_mood.text: Alright? Grab a pint or a coffee, because the macro picture is looking increasingly spicy. Between US inflation refusing to play ball, oil creeping past $100, and central bankers dusting off their hawkish feathers, it's been a week of reality checks in the City. Today, we're unpacking why the Fed might be about to pull the ultimate walk of shame, how to unlock millions by drawing a line down a balance sheet, and why almost every academic paper claiming 'AI alpha' is a work of fiction. Let's get into it.

content.text: The Fed's U-Turn? Hot US Inflation Teases a Shock Rate Hike

What happened: US August CPI rose 0.4% month-on-month (3.4% y-o-y), with core CPI ticking up 0.3% (2.4% y-o-y)—slightly hotter than the 0.2% consensus. This followed a spicy PPI print of 0.4% monthly (5.4% y-o-y). With the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting next week on September 16, markets have suddenly ramped up the implied probability of a 25 bps rate hike to around 70%. If they pull the trigger, it will be the first hike since summer 2023, reversing a two-year easing cycle that had brought the target range down from 5.50% to 3.50%–3.75%.

Why it matters: Reversing a cutting cycle to hike rates is the ultimate central banking walk of shame. It tells the market that the Fed lost control of the narrative and that supply-side shocks are winning. Adding fuel to the fire, political promises of $5,000 fiscal stimulus checks ahead of the US midterms have pushed inflation expectations (TIPS breakevens) to their highest levels since June.

The City angle: For fixed-income desks, the two-year Treasury yield jumping 15 bps to a two-year high is a brutal reminder that the 'duration trade' is still a minefield. If you've been blindly buying bonds expecting a smooth ride down in yields, you're currently licking your wounds.

What to say at work: 'If Warsh actually hikes next week, it’s a massive regime shift. They’ve spent two years cutting rates, and a hike now is an admission that inflation is structurally sticky, driven by geopolitical energy shocks and pre-election fiscal bribes. It’s going to be a wild FOMC meeting.'
Lagarde’s Line in the Sand: ECB Hikes to 2.5% on Energy Fears

What happened: The European Central Bank raised its key deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%—its second hike this year. President Christine Lagarde warned that Middle East conflict-driven energy pressures are 'longer lasting than we had anticipated,' with the bank revising its 2027 inflation forecast up to 2.5%. Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, and Barclays are already forecasting further hikes in December.

Why it matters: Despite eurozone growth being revised up only marginally to 0.9% for 2026, the ECB made it clear that inflation is the enemy. Lagarde stated that the rate hike stands even under a 'severe energy shock scenario.' They are prioritising credibility over growth, even if it tips the eurozone into a technical recession.

The City angle: Sovereign debt is taking a beating. The German 10-year Bund yield touched 3.44% (the highest since 2011). If you're managing a multi-asset portfolio, the classic 60/40 is hurting as both equities and bonds feel the squeeze of sticky, supply-side inflation.

What to say at work: 'Lagarde is prioritising credibility over growth. With Dutch wholesale gas passing ‐80/MWh and Brent crude hovering over $100, the ECB is terrified of second-round wage-price spirals. They’d rather trigger a mild recession than let inflation expectations unanchor.'
July GDP Surprise: The UK Economy Refuses to Play Dead

What happened: UK GDP expanded by 0.4% month-on-month in July, comfortably beating expectations of a flat 0.0% print and building on June’s 0.3% growth. Services and production both showed resilience, helping the FTSE 100 snap a five-day losing streak to close up 0.39% at 10,650.44.

Why it matters: While a stronger economy is great news for the high street, it’s a headache for the Bank of England (meeting on September 17). The ONS data suggests the UK has carried its first-half momentum into Q3, which gives policymakers very little room to stay on hold if energy-driven inflation starts creeping back into services. Markets are already pricing in a November hike to 4.0%.

The City angle: UK domestic banks (NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds) rallied between 1.3% and 2.0% on the news, benefiting from the prospect of higher-for-longer net interest margins. However, Gilt yields hit a 19-year high, meaning anyone holding long-duration UK sovereign debt is having a miserable month.

What to say at work: 'The 0.4% July GDP print is a double-edged sword. It’s great for UK plc’s earnings, but it completely strips away any dovish cover for the Bank of England. If the ECB is hiking and the Fed is contemplating a U-turn, the BoE is almost certainly going to have to follow suit in November.'
The Tanker War in the Gulf: US-Iran Skirmishes Send Brent Crude Past $100

What happened: Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East escalated dramatically after the U.S. destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for a missile fired at a U.S. warship. Brent crude touched $107 per barrel and WTI hit $102 earlier in the week, before easing slightly to around $104 on Friday after the IEA downgraded global demand forecasts.

Why it matters: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most important oil chokepoint. With the Houthis also extending their reach toward the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, shipping insurance, freight rates, and wholesale gas prices are soaring. British wholesale gas topped 203p per therm, the highest since December 2022.

The City angle: This is a classic stagflationary shock. Commodity trading desks and macro hedge funds are printing money, but for equity and credit analysts, it means rising input costs, squeezed margins, and a higher cost of capital across the board.

What to say at work: 'The tanker clashes are a stark reminder of why supply-side energy shocks are a central banker's worst nightmare. You can't interest-rate-hike your way to more oil tankers or safer shipping lanes, but you have to hike anyway to suppress aggregate demand and stop inflation from spiralling.'
Lilly Buys AtaiBeckley: GLP-1 Cash Meets the Mind

What happened: Eli Lilly and Company completed its acquisition of AtaiBeckley Inc., a clinical-stage biopharma company developing rapid-acting neuroplastogens for mental health conditions, including a promising treatment for treatment-resistant depression (BPL-003).

Why it matters: Big Pharma is sitting on mountains of cash—especially Lilly and Novo Nordisk, thanks to their blockbuster GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. As traditional blockbusters face patent cliffs, giants are aggressively deploying this capital into high-barrier neuroscience and oncology.

The City angle: For healthcare investment bankers and biotech venture capitalists, this is a massive green shoot. It proves that strategic buyers are willing to pay hefty premiums for clinical-stage assets with strong IP, even in a high-rate environment.

What to say at work: 'Lilly’s acquisition of AtaiBeckley is a textbook example of big pharma recycling its obesity cash cows into the next frontier of medicine. Neuroscience is the new oncology—high risk, but the addressable market for treatment-resistant depression is astronomical.'
AI Safety Gets Real: Anthropic Thwarts Bio-Weapon Prompts

What happened: Anthropic released a threat intelligence report revealing it had actively blocked attempts by bad actors to use its Claude models to assist in the creation of biological weapons. This comes amid growing warnings from former top researchers about the existential risks of frontier AI models.

Why it matters: AI safety and 'red-teaming' are moving from academic talking points to hard operational realities. As models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude's latest iterations roll out, the regulatory scrutiny on LLM providers is intensifying.

The City angle: For tech VCs and growth equity investors, safety compliance is no longer just a PR exercise—it’s a major operational cost and a potential regulatory bottleneck. If governments impose strict licensing or liability on frontier model developers, it could severely impact the valuations and rollout speeds of these multi-billion-dollar AI startups.

What to say at work: 'Anthropic’s report shows why AI safety is going to become a massive compliance burden. If model providers are legally liable for what their LLMs help users build, we’re going to see a lot of friction in enterprise rollouts. It’s a key risk factor to price into any AI infrastructure play.'

content.text: The Return of the Hawk: Warsh, Oil, and the 5% Yield Threat

September is living up to its reputation as an absolute shocker for risk assets. While Friday saw a decent relief rally—the S&P 500 clawing back 0.86% to close at 7,656.98 as oil prices eased slightly—the weekly tape tells a much grimmer story. For the week, the S&P 500 was down 0.68%, the Dow lost 1.51%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 dipped 0.52%. But under the hood, the engine is making some very funny noises. The equal-weight S&P 500 gave up 1.87% and small caps (Russell 2000) got absolutely battered, down 2.38%. When the average stock is falling three times as hard as the main index, you aren't looking at a healthy market; you're looking at a handful of mega-cap tech names carrying a very heavy, very tired basket.
The Oil Shock and the Fed's Reversal

The culprit behind this week's jitters is a classic supply-side energy shock. Escalating US-Iran tensions in the Middle East saw WTI crude oil surge to $100 a barrel, with Brent crude hovering above $104. That energy spike fed straight into the macro data. August CPI showed core inflation rising 0.3% month-on-month (above the 0.2% expected), while headline annual CPI remained sticky at 3.4%. On the wholesale side, PPI jumped 0.4% on the month, pushing the annual rate to a spicy 5.4%. This has given the bond market the perfect excuse to price in an 85%+ chance of a rate hike at the upcoming FOMC meeting on September 16.

If new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh pulls the trigger next week, it will be a 25-basis-point hike to a 3.75%–4.00% range. This would be the first rate hike since the summer of 2023, completely reversing the two-year easing cycle. Warsh already warned us at Jackson Hole in August that 'price stability is not self-executing'. He is famously a man of few words who wants a 'quieter, more purposeful Fed'—and right now, his silence is sounding incredibly hawkish.
The Cross-Asset Read: Yields at the Gates of 5%

The real drama is playing out in fixed income. The 10-year US Treasury yield jumped nearly 20 basis points this week to close just under 5%—flirting with three-year highs. It wasn't just inflation driving the move; a disappointing Treasury buyback ($6 billion announced versus the expected $10 billion) left the market digesting more supply than it wanted. When long yields spike like this, it's a signal that the market thinks a single 'one-and-done' hike from Warsh won't be enough to tame the energy-driven inflation beast.

items: The First Hike is Rarely the Problem: Historically, the initial rate hike of a cycle doesn't kill equities—the S&P 500 has averaged a 5.7% gain in the six months following the first hike of the last eight cycles. The real danger is the pace of what follows. If the 10-year yield breaks cleanly above 5%, expect equity valuations to get squeezed hard.

The Cash Trap: With money market funds yielding around 3.5% and inflation running at 3.4%, real returns on cash are practically flat. Once you factor in taxes on interest, the 'VOO and chill' crowd is realising that hiding in cash is a guaranteed way to lose purchasing power.

Divergent Tech Resilience: Despite the rate pressure, AI-adjacent names are showing bizarre strength. Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Qualcomm both rallied this week on AI infrastructure optimism and AWS partnerships. The institutional view is clear: the AI capex train is moving too fast to be derailed by a 25 bps hike.

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The OpCo/PropCo Split

content.text: The OpCo/PropCo Split: Financial Engineering or Just Moving the Deckchairs?

Imagine you own a successful chain of pubs across London. You own the buildings, and you pour the pints. To the untrained eye, you run a pub business. To a private equity analyst or a clever corporate financier, you are sitting on a goldmine of mispriced assets. This is where the OpCo/PropCo (Operating Company / Property Company) split comes in.

At its core, an OpCo/PropCo split involves carving a business into two distinct corporate entities. 'PropCo' takes ownership of the physical real estate (the land and buildings), while 'OpCo' owns the brand, the inventory, the staff, and the actual day-to-day operations. OpCo then signs long-term master leases to rent the properties back from PropCo.
The Cost-of-Capital Arbitrage

Why bother with all this paperwork? It comes down to cost of capital and multiple arbitrage. Real estate and operating businesses have fundamentally different risk profiles, and therefore, different investor bases. Real estate investors want stable, bond-like yields and are willing to accept lower returns (a lower cost of capital). Operating investors want growth and are willing to take operational risk, but demand a higher return. By splitting them, you let each investor buy exactly what they want.
Let's look at the maths of how this unlocks value:

items: The Integrated Business: Your pub chain generates �100m in EBITDA. Because pub operations are risky and cyclical, the market values the integrated business at an 8x EBITDA multiple, giving it an Enterprise Value (EV) of �800m.
The Split: You create PropCo and OpCo. PropCo charges OpCo �60m a year in rent. OpCo's EBITDA drops from �100m to �40m (after paying the rent).

Valuing PropCo: PropCo now has �60m of highly predictable, inflation-linked rental income backed by hard real estate. Real estate investors love this and value it at a 6.5% cap rate (equivalent to a 15.4x multiple). PropCo is suddenly worth �923m.
Valuing OpCo: OpCo is now an asset-light operating business making �40m. Even if the market penalises its higher operational risk and values it at a lower 5x multiple, OpCo is worth �200m.

The Result: By simply drawing a line down the middle of the balance sheet, you have turned an �800m business into a combined �1.123bn of value (�923m PropCo + �200m OpCo). That is a �323m (40%) value unlock without selling a single extra pint.

content.text: Why It Matters in Asset Management and Private Equity

This isn't just academic. It is a staple playbook for private equity firms investing in real-estate-heavy sectors like hotels, supermarkets, care homes, and pub estates. By separating the real estate, the PE firm can execute a 'sale-leaseback'—selling the PropCo to a Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) or a pension fund to instantly raise cheap capital. This cash can be used to pay down acquisition debt, fund growth, or pay themselves a fat dividend, all while retaining the high-growth, asset-light operating business.
The Common Pitfall: The Leverage Trap

The classic beginner mistake is thinking this is a free lunch. It isn't. Rent is a fixed cost. By turning owned property into leased property, you are replacing equity with operating leverage. If pub revenues drop by 20%, your rent doesn't drop. Under modern accounting standards (IFRS 16 / ASC 842), these leases are capitalised on the balance sheet as debt-like liabilities anyway, so sophisticated analysts won't be fooled into thinking the business is truly 'debt-free'.

Many UK high street names and care home operators (like Southern Cross in the past) have been driven into administration because their OpCos couldn't meet the rigid rent payments demanded by their PropCos during a downturn.
How to Use This in Interviews

If you are interviewing for a role in real estate private equity, generalist PE, or investment banking, this is a killer concept to explain clearly. If asked how to unlock value in an asset-heavy retail or leisure business, walk them through the OpCo/PropCo split.

"To impress, you might say: 'While an OpCo/PropCo split can unlock massive value by exploiting the yield spread between real estate and operating cash flows, it fundamentally increases the operational gearing of the OpCo. In a downturn, those fixed lease payments act exactly like debt service, meaning you've essentially leveraged the business through the back door. You have to ensure the master lease is structured with enough flexibility—like CPI caps or variable rent components—to prevent OpCo from suffocating.'"

content.text: The Idea: SABR-Informed Multitask Gaussian Process (SABR-MTGP)

Constructing a smooth, arbitrage-free implied volatility surface (IVS) is one of the most fundamental challenges in derivatives trading. If you rely purely on classical parametric models like SABR (Stochastic Alpha Beta Rho), you get robust, mathematically consistent wings, but you lack the flexibility to capture local market idiosyncrasies or complex term structures. If you go full machine learning with standard Gaussian Processes (GPs) or neural networks, you get incredible flexibility, but the model easily overfits, behaves wildly in data-scarce regions (like deep out-of-the-money strikes), and can easily violate no-arbitrage conditions. The SABR-Informed Multitask Gaussian Process (SABR-MTGP) solves this by framing IVS construction as a multi-task learning problem: using a dense, synthetic SABR-generated surface as a 'source task' to guide a sparse, noisy market-data 'target task'.
How It Works

Instead of fitting a GP directly to sparse market quotes, we train a Multitask GP on two distinct datasets simultaneously. Task 0 is a dense, synthetic grid of implied volatilities generated from a calibrated SABR model. This synthetic dataset acts as a structural prior, embedding the physical laws of option pricing (like asymptotic wing behavior and basic arbitrage constraints). Task 1 is the actual, sparse, and noisy market option quotes. By using a multitask covariance kernel, the GP learns the correlation between the theoretical SABR surface and the real market. In regions with abundant market data, the GP flexibly adapts to empirical reality. In data-scarce regions (such as deep OTM or long-dated options), the model gracefully falls back to the SABR-guided structure, preventing unrealistic extrapolations and preserving no-arbitrage conditions.
A Mini Technical Example in Python
Here is how you can structure a Multitask GP for this using a GPyTorch-style framework. We use an IndexKernel to model the cross-task covariance between the SABR prior and the real market data.

import torch
import gpytorch

class SABRMultitaskGP(gpytorch.models.ExactGP):
    def __init__(self, train_x, train_y, likelihood, num_tasks=2):
        super().__init__(train_x, train_y, likelihood)
        # Mean module for the surface
        self.mean_module = gpytorch.means.ConstantMean()
        # Spatial kernel over option features: log-moneyness and time-to-maturity
        self.covar_module = gpytorch.kernels.RBFKernel()
        # Task kernel to learn correlation between SABR (Task 0) and Market (Task 1)
        self.task_covar_module = gpytorch.kernels.IndexKernel(num_tasks=num_tasks, rank=1)

    def forward(self, x, task_indices):
        mean_x = self.mean_module(x)
        covar_x = self.covar_module(x)
        # Combine spatial covariance with task-specific correlation
        covar_task = self.task_covar_module(task_indices)
        covar = covar_x * covar_task
        return gpytorch.distributions.MultivariateNormal(mean_x, covar)
The Paper Angle

This approach is detailed in the paper 'SABR-Informed Multitask Gaussian Process: A Synthetic-to-Real Framework for Implied Volatility Surface Construction' (arXiv:2506.22888, revised Feb 2026) by Jirong Zhuang and Xuan Wu. The authors demonstrate that by learning the cross-task dependence via task embeddings with hierarchical regularization, the SABR-MTGP significantly outperforms both standard single-task GPs and pure SABR models. It is particularly effective at near-term maturities where market data is notoriously noisy, while remaining highly competitive and structurally sound at long-term maturities.
The Pub / Interview Conversation

If you are interviewing for a quant research or derivatives trading role, this is a brilliant concept to bring up when asked about the limits of machine learning in pricing. You can say: 'Purely data-driven models for implied volatility surfaces often fail because they don't respect financial priors, leading to arbitrage or wild extrapolation in the wings. Instead of just throwing a neural network at the problem, a more elegant approach is a synthetic-to-real framework. By using a Multitask Gaussian Process, we can treat a dense, calibrated SABR surface as a source task and the sparse market data as the target task. This lets the model learn the empirical deviations from SABR where data is rich, while safely falling back to SABR's robust asymptotic behavior where data is scarce.'
Risks and Limitations

While elegant, GPs suffer from cubic computational complexity, O(N^3), with respect to the number of data points. If you are fitting intraday surfaces across thousands of strikes and maturities, you will need to employ sparse GP approximations or Kronecker-structured covariances to keep latency low. Additionally, if the underlying SABR model is poorly calibrated or if there is a massive regime shift that violates SABR's assumptions entirely, the 'source task' could introduce unwanted bias into your target market predictions.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading: The Five Sins of Financial AI

content.text: The Five Sins of Financial AI

If you spend any time on LinkedIn or reading sell-side tech pitches, you have probably seen a dozen claims about how some new Large Language Model (LLM) is 'beating the market' or 'delivering 40% annualised alpha.' It all sounds brilliant until you try to run it with real money and watch your capital evaporate. A fantastic paper from researchers at Oxford, Florida, Chicago Booth, and BlackRock explains exactly why this happens. It is called 'Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration' (Kong et al., 2026).

The authors reviewed 164 academic papers published between 2023 and 2025 that claimed to use LLMs for financial trading or analysis. The punchline? Almost all of them are built on a house of cards. The paper identifies what it calls the 'five sins' of financial LLM evaluation—structural biases that systematically inflate performance and create a massive 'illusion of validity.' It is like buying a pint of 'award-winning' craft lager only to find out the brewer judged it themselves in their own kitchen.
The Five Sins

items: Look-Ahead Bias (The Cheat Sheet): This comes in two flavours. First, 'parametric leakage'—if an LLM's training cutoff is late 2025, and you backtest it on 2024 data, it isn't predicting Nvidia's earnings; it is just reading its own memory. It is like sitting an exam with the answer sheet open. Second, 'external leakage'—Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often pull from databases or live search results that have been retrospectively updated with future information.

Survivorship Bias (The Ghost Town): Most evaluations only test the LLM on companies that are currently in the index (like the S&P 500 today). They completely ignore the companies that went bust, got acquired, or delisted during the backtest period. It is easy to look like a stock-picking genius when you have silently deleted all the losers from your test set.

Narrative Bias (The Monday Morning Quarterback): LLMs are trained to be coherent storytellers. When asked to justify a trade, they will construct a beautifully logical, highly persuasive narrative using information that simply was not available or relevant at the time of the decision. They are brilliant at hallucinating a neat story after the fact.

Objective Bias (The Overconfident Bullshitter): Standard LLM training (like RLHF) rewards models for being helpful and confident. In finance, the correct answer is often 'the data is too noisy, I do not know.' LLMs are structurally biased against admitting uncertainty, leading them to hallucinate high-conviction recommendations on pure noise because they are programmed to please.

Cost Bias (The Spreadsheet Fantasy): Many backtests assume zero transaction costs, zero market impact, zero borrow costs, and zero latency. Even worse, they ignore the actual API costs of running millions of LLM tokens, which can easily wipe out any theoretical alpha. Your model might make 2% on paper, but if the OpenAI bill is 3%, you are just funding Sam Altman's next data centre.

content.text: Why This Matters for the City

This is not just academic nitpicking; it is a massive commercial issue. Out of the 164 papers the authors reviewed, look-ahead bias was only acknowledged in 26.8% of them, and survivorship bias was mentioned in a pathetic 1.2%. If the smartest minds in academic machine learning are routinely making these basic errors, you can bet your life that the vendors pitching to your fund are doing the same.
These sins often stack. They create an illusion of validity where strong numbers coexist with invalid backtests and systems that cannot be deployed.
How to Use This at Work

The next time a junior analyst or an external vendor pitches you an 'AI-driven trading strategy' or an 'automated analyst workflow,' do not get blinded by the charts. Use this paper as your BS-detector. Ask them three simple questions:

items: What was the exact training cutoff date of the model, and does it overlap with your backtest period?
How did you construct your historical universe? Did you include delisted and bankrupt firms?
What are the estimated API token costs per trade, and are they factored into the net PnL?

content.text: If they look like a deer in headlights, you have just saved your firm a lot of money and embarrassment.
What to Skim and What to Read

You can safely skim the heavy machine-learning math in the 'Structural Validity Framework' section. Instead, focus your attention on Section 2, which details the five biases, and the excellent checklist in the appendix. It is a ready-made audit tool for any financial AI project.

sections.title: People / Business Psychology: The Short Email Panic

content.text: The Short Email Panic: Hostile Attribution Bias

We've all been there. It's 5:30 PM on a Thursday, and your Managing Director sends a five-word email: 'Come see me tomorrow morning.' No context. No exclamation mark. Just a cold, hard full stop. Your brain immediately enters threat-detection mode. You spend the evening sweating, mentally auditing every financial model you've touched this month, convinced you've double-counted EBITDA or committed some other career-ending error. You turn up to their office the next morning defensive, armed with a 20-slide justification deck, only for the MD to look up and say: 'Great work on that pitch, I just wanted to see if we can copy the slide layout for the next client.'

This cognitive glitch is known as Hostile Attribution Bias (HAB). It's the psychological tendency to interpret ambiguous, neutral, or clumsy actions from others as deliberate, targeted hostility. Research by industrial-organisational psychologist Paul Spector shows that HAB is one of the single biggest predictors of workplace conflict. When we're under stress, our brains naturally default to a defensive crouch, treating every brief email, missed greeting in the corridor, or constructive piece of feedback as a personal attack.

In the City, this bias runs rampant. Take the classic friction between the Front Office and Risk. When a risk analyst flags a portfolio's VaR limit, the Portfolio Manager's immediate reaction is often: 'These guys are deliberately trying to block my trades and ruin my PnL.' In reality, the risk analyst doesn't care about the PM's personal vendettas; they're simply ticking a compliance box required by the regulator so they can go home on time.

How can you use this to your advantage? First, apply Hanlon's Razor: never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by busyness, distraction, or a desperate need for a coffee. If you receive a blunt email, pause before you draft a passive-aggressive essay in response. Assume neutral intent. Second, this is a goldmine for interviews. When asked how you handle difficult stakeholders or resolve team conflicts, explain that you actively manage Hostile Attribution Bias. It shows an elite level of emotional intelligence and commercial maturity to say: 'I always assume positive intent in written communication because emails lack tone, and people are usually just busy, not angry.'
One line to remember
They aren't out to get you; they're just busy, distracted, or desperately need a coffee.
